newsitem.title: USA: Energy Dept lost $500 million of property - report.
newsitem.headline: Energy Dept lost $500 million of property - report.

text.p: Trying to catch the eye of the next energy secretary, Sen. John Glenn of Ohio Wednesday released a report compiling some $500 million in losses over the years from poor inventory management at the Energy Department.

"For a number of years, I have conducted and initiated a number of investigations and surveys into DOE's (Department of Energy) ability to oversee its vast inventory," Glenn, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Governmental Affairs Committee, said in a statement.
"This report alone points out a total of up to $500 million of missing, misinventoried, and improperly disposed of property we've discovered in just the past 10 years," he said.
Besides wasted tax dollars, Glenn said the report showed the department's poor management led to the government losing control of some dangerous military equipment.
Glenn sent the report, which his spokesman said compiled findings that mostly have been disclosed before, to the Senate Energy Committee.
That panel was to hold a confirmation hearing on Thursday on Federico Pena, who was seeking a job change from transportation secretary to energy secretary.
"This happened under Republican and Democratic administrations. We want assurances from the Energy Department that these problems will get their attention," Glenn's spokesman said.

Examples of losses were some $33 million in missing or unaccounted-for equipment at the Rocky Flats nuclear weapons site in Colorado, and 4,000 rounds of ammunition lost at the Savannah River facility in South Carolina.
Glenn said he was particularly concerned that the department tighten its inventory control before it starts an assets disposition and sales programme that is supposed to net $110 million by 2003.

His report recommended creating a central office to oversee property management of the department's far-flung operations, holding contractors and civil service personnel accountable for property management abuses, and using strong property management rules in department contracts.
